prize_parts.citation: for the proposal and realisation of the optical lattice clock, in which many atoms are trapped at a magic wavelength, and for its development to a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18, opening new tests of gravity, fundamental constants and dark matter

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: one part, B001, Katori and Ye. After the whole first round every one of us names exactly this part and these two names, so the remaining work is to make the citation exact and to test the objections, not to choose between rivals. The scientific core is the magic-wavelength lattice. Atoms are held so tightly that Doppler and recoil shifts vanish, thousands are interrogated at once, and the trap light shifts the two clock levels equally so that the perturbation cancels. Once the collisional and blackbody shifts were understood, the clock reached 10^-18. At that level the clock sees gravitational time dilation across a millimetre-sized sample and sets limits on varying constants and ultralight dark matter. That is quantum mechanics of atoms understood to the last digit. Independent laboratories reproduce and compare these clocks, so it is not a single-measurement claim. The two names are the identifiable decisive steps: Katori for the proposal and first realisation, Ye for taking it to record accuracy and stability with new many-body clock physics.
statement.case_against: The strongest objection, which I raised myself and which the chair puts first, is that this is a refinement of areas already honoured, the frequency comb in 2005 and the control of single quantum systems and ion clocks in 2012. I still answer that the lattice clock rests on a different principle, but I accept that this answer must be written into the citation, which is why it names the lattice and the magic wavelength and not clocks in general. Second, a two-name credit leaves out Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom, Hinkley, Campbell and the Paris, NIST and PTB teams, and none of us has verified the priority record, myself included. Third, 10^-18 can be read as a record in systematic control, as Eva Olsson says, and the largest application, the redefined second, has not yet arrived. These weigh on the margins of attribution and timing, but I do not think they touch the physical discovery.

responses.point: Eva Olsson says the headline 10^-18 result is close to a record in systematic uncertainty and that the case depends on whether the proposal and first lattice clock are the invention and not the later record accuracy.
responses.response: I think this is the sharpest point raised in round 1 and I would answer it by putting both in the citation, as invention and development, not by choosing between them. Without the magic-wavelength idea there is no clock to push to 10^-18, and without the work of understanding lattice-induced and collisional shifts the idea would have remained a proposal. The reason I do not read 10^-18 as only a record is that the systematic control is itself physics: spin-polarised fermions, many-body interactions between atoms in a lattice, and blackbody shifts. The new observations that follow, millimetre-scale redshift and bounds on constants, could not be made before. I agree that if the committee wished to honour only the original idea, Katori's name alone would be the natural reading, and I would not support that because the demonstration of the full potential is Ye's.

responses.point: The chair asks which citation wording states the lattice concept without claiming optical clocks in general, and whether the SI second redefinition should affect timing.
responses.response: My proposed wording names the optical lattice clock and the magic-wavelength trapping explicitly, and gives the 10^-18 level and the tests of gravity, constants and dark matter as consequences, so that nobody can read it as a prize for optical clocks as such or for frequency metrology, which are already recognised. On timing I keep my first-round position: the redefinition is a decision for the metrology community that follows the physics, and waiting would tie the prize to a committee process outside physics. It is also true that the best clocks now outperform the caesium definition, which is itself a sign that the discovery is mature. I would accept the chair's concern as a reason for care in wording, not for delay.

responses.point: Stefan treats B042 as the strongest second option but asks whether a two-part prize adding B042 or B003 would improve the configuration or only dilute it, given the three-person limit.
responses.response: I have thought about this again and I do not move to two parts. B042 is the strongest second candidate, but the three-person cap forces a choice among Bloch, Cirac, Greiner, Zoller and Esslinger, and the theory proposal by Zoller and Cirac and the experiments in Munich and Zurich need different recognition. Any three would leave out two people whose claims are comparable, and I would not want to hand the committee a part that we have to defend by counting names. Adding it would also push B001 down to two people sharing a configuration of five, which does not serve a clean prize. B003 raises the same allocation problem and a closeness to last year's prize. I would keep B042 as an alternative for a later year when the credit question has been worked through.

responses.point: Bernhard moved from B006 to B001 and asks whether other clock groups have claims strong enough to displace or join Katori and Ye, noting that he cannot verify the priority record.
responses.response: I agree that this is the open factual question, and I should be plain that it is not answered by any of us on the basis of memory. As far as I can judge from the literature that I know, the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice clock are Katori's, and the path to the lowest systematic uncertainty and instability runs through Ye's laboratory, with the Paris and other groups close behind and not in front. That is why I would join you in asking the committee's external reviewers to check priority before the vote and not rely on our recollection. I do not see it as a reason to add a third name: Lemonde, Ludlow, Bloom and Hinkley each carried an important step but none of them is the origin of the concept or the single leader in precision, and adding one would reopen the question of the others.

responses.point: Ulf lists B045 and B017 as alternatives and rests his support on nature itself checking the clock result, with attribution cleaner than elsewhere on the shortlist.
responses.response: I agree on the point that nature does the checking here, since clocks in different laboratories agree and the gravitational redshift is measured, not modelled. On B017, where we share an alternative, I would keep it behind: magic-angle graphene is under ten years old and the pairing mechanism is unresolved, which is a scientific question that we cannot treat as a footnote. I would not use it to build a second part. B045 is outside my field and I defer to you and Mark on it, but the attribution problem you raise with van Paradijs and Piro seems to me to be of the same type as the one we have for the clock groups.

uncertainties: Whether the committee, after reading the chair's questions, accepts the lattice clock as a distinct discovery and not as a continuation of the 2005 and 2012 prizes. I think it is distinct, but this is a judgment and not a fact.

The priority record for the magic-wavelength proposal, the first strontium lattice clock and the first 10^-18 result is not independently verified by me. I rely on general knowledge, and an external check would be welcome.
Whether two names is defensible when other groups made decisive steps. I believe it is, but the three-person cap forces the omission.
For B042 and B017, my alternatives, which names would be defended: for B042 I could not choose three of five with confidence, and for B017 the pairing mechanism is not resolved.
statement.conflict_note: I am a long-time close collaborator of Anne L'Huillier (2023 laureate) and have co-authored with the Lund and ETH attosecond groups. None of Katori or Ye is among my collaborators, and none of the credited names for the shortlisted ballots is on my list of collaborators. My connection to B001 and B042 is at the level of the field only, as I work in atomic theory. This is unchanged from round 1, and I do not see a reason to recuse myself. I note that Goran Johansson has stated that he should recuse himself from B003, which I do not propose.
